hints: Picture what a Group 2 metal looks like at particle level, a regular arrangement of positive ions surrounded by mobile electrons from the outer s orbitals.
Recall the single word Cambridge always requires for the type of attraction in metallic, ionic and covalent bonding.
walkthrough:
Visualise the metal lattice**
Think of Group 2 atoms losing their two outer s electrons. You are left with $\text{M}^{2+}$ ions packed in a regular lattice, with those lost electrons free to move everywhere between them. They are no longer tied to one atom, so we call them delocalised.

Name the attraction correctly**
Bonding is always electrostatic attraction between opposite charges. Here it is the attraction of the positive ions for the negative delocalised electron sea in all directions. State both sides clearly: positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.
Final answer: Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions / cations and delocalised electrons.

hints: Compare $\text{Be}^{2+}$ at the top of Group 2 with $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ at the bottom and count how many occupied electron shells each ion keeps.
Link the addition of a new principal shell to the distance from the nucleus to the outer electrons.
walkthrough:
State the trend with confidence**
Down Group 2 from $\text{Be}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ the ions get larger. Even though nuclear charge increases, the size effect of adding shells dominates.

Explain with shells**
Each step down adds a new principal quantum shell, for example $n=2$ to $n=3$ to $n=4$. The outer electrons are further from the nucleus, so the radius of the $2+$ ion increases.

Final answer: Ionic radius increases down Group 2.
Each successive element has an extra occupied electron shell.

hints: Look at the numbers 900 to 1760 to 14800, note the steady rise then the very large jump, and think about what happens to charge and distance after each electron is removed.
Recall the electron configuration of Be, $1s^2 2s^2$, and decide which shell the 1st, 2nd and 3rd electrons come from.
walkthrough:
Explain the general increase**
Each electron removed leaves fewer electrons to repel each other, so there is less shielding. The remaining electrons are pulled closer, the ion gets smaller, and the nucleus attracts the next electron more strongly. That is why $900 < 1760 < 14800 < 21000$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Spot the shell change**
Beryllium is $1s^2 2s^2$. The 1st and 2nd electrons both come from the $n=2$ outer shell, so the rise is small. The 3rd electron must be taken from the $n=1$ inner shell, much closer to the nucleus and with no inner shielding, so far more energy is needed. That huge jump confirms Be has 2 outer electrons and forms $\text{Be}^{2+}$.

Final answer: Ionisation energies increase because of less shielding / smaller successive ionic radii / greater attraction of the electron to the nucleus.
The large jump between 2nd and 3rd IE is because the 3rd electron is removed from an inner shell / lower energy level.

hints: Compare the relative masses of protons, neutrons and electrons, about 1, 1 and 1/1840.
Recall where each subatomic particle is located in the atom.
walkthrough:
Weigh the particles**
A proton and a neutron each have a relative mass of about 1, while an electron is about 1/1840, essentially negligible. So almost all the mass comes from protons plus neutrons.

Locate that mass**
In $^{9}_{4}\text{Be}$ the 4 protons and 5 neutrons sit packed together in the tiny central nucleus, with only 4 almost massless electrons outside. Therefore essentially all the mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

Final answer: Most of the mass is in the nucleus.
Because protons and neutrons / nucleons are found in the nucleus.

hints: Remember isotopes of the same element have the same atomic number, so find Z for magnesium from the Periodic Table.
Use neutrons = mass number minus protons for 24, 25 and 26.
walkthrough:
Fix the proton number**
Isotopes are the same element, so proton number never changes. Magnesium has $Z = 12$, so every isotope has 12 protons.

Calculate neutrons by subtraction**
Use $\text{neutrons} = A - Z$. For $^{24}\text{Mg}$: $24 - 12 = 12$. For $^{25}\text{Mg}$: $25 - 12 = 13$. For $^{26}\text{Mg}$: $26 - 12 = 14$.

Final answer: number of protons = 12 for magnesium-24, magnesium-25 and magnesium-26.
number of neutrons = 12 for magnesium-24, 13 for magnesium-25 and 14 for magnesium-26.

hints: Decide how a neutral particle responds to charged plates compared with the positively charged proton beam shown.
Decide which plate a negative particle will be attracted to, opposite to the proton beam.
Compare the mass of an electron with a proton at the same velocity to judge the size of deflection.
walkthrough:
Draw the neutron beam**
Neutrons have no charge, so the electric field exerts no force on them. Draw a straight horizontal line straight on from the source, continuing without bending up or down. Label it neutrons.

Draw the electron beam direction**
Electrons are negative, opposite to protons. The proton beam bends up toward the negative plate, so electrons bend down toward the positive plate. Draw a curving line from the same source bending downwards. Label it electrons.

Show the greater deflection**
Deflection depends on charge to mass ratio. An electron and a proton have equal but opposite charge magnitude, but the electron mass is about 1/1840 of a proton. At the same velocity it is deflected much more, so your electron curve must be steeper and further from the centre than the proton curve.

Final answer: Neutron beam: horizontal straight line from same source, undeflected.
Electron beam: curving line deflected downwards / to positive plate from same source.
Electron deflection is greater / larger than proton beam deflection.

hints: Think what you would see when a white basic oxide neutralises dilute acid to form soluble $\text{BaCl}_2$ with no gas product.
Think what extra observation appears when carbonate ions react with $\text{H}^{+}$ to give $\text{CO}_2$ gas.
walkthrough:
Observe barium oxide plus acid**
$\text{BaO} + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{BaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. This is simple neutralisation with no gas. You see the white solid dissolve to give a colourless solution.

Observe barium carbonate plus acid**
$\text{BaCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{BaCl}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The solid also dissolves, but carbonate gives carbon dioxide, so you also see fizzing or effervescence. Both points are needed for the mark.

Final answer: barium oxide: (white) solid disappears / dissolves.
Barium carbonate: effervescence AND (white) solid disappears / dissolves.

hints: Recall the general pattern: Group 2 metal plus water gives metal hydroxide plus hydrogen, and check the formula of strontium hydroxide.
walkthrough:
Build and balance the equation**
Strontium is like calcium but more reactive. It gives $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$. You need two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to supply two $\text{OH}$ groups and balance H: $$\text{Sr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Sr(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2$$

hints: Recall the test for sulfate with $\text{BaCl}_2$ works because barium sulfate is the least soluble, then extend that trend down the group.
walkthrough:
Remember the solubility pattern**
Group 2 sulfates become less soluble going down: $\text{MgSO}_4$ is very soluble, $\text{CaSO}_4$ sparingly soluble, $\text{SrSO}_4$ and $\text{BaSO}_4$ are insoluble. That is why $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ precipitates sulfate so reliably. So solubility decreases down the group.
Final answer: Solubility decreases down the group.
